opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest test I use is to ask: if the next generation of models is ten times better, does this company get stronger or does it disappear? There's a whole category of startups that are basically patching the weaknesses of today's models. Maybe the model can't do long context well, or it hallucinates on some format, or it can't follow a complex workflow, and so someone builds a clever scaffolding layer around it. That can be a great product for twelve months, but you're essentially betting against the progress curve, and I've seen that bet lose again and again. Every time we trained a new model, a bunch of those workarounds just became unnecessary.

The companies I'm more optimistic about are the ones where a better model is a tailwind. If your product is built so that every improvement in reasoning or coding or tool use flows directly to your users, then you're riding the wave instead of fighting it. Coding assistants are a good example: the better the model, the more useful the product, and the company is accumulating something that isn't just the model, the workflow, the integration into how developers actually work, the trust, the distribution.

So I look at what they own that the model provider doesn't. Is it proprietary data that keeps compounding? Is it a feedback loop from real usage, where they learn what users actually want and can turn that into evaluation sets or fine-tuning signals? Is it deep integration into some vertical, legal, medical, finance, where knowing the domain, the regulations, and the customers is the hard part? Those things don't get commoditized when GPT or Llama or Claude gets better.

The other question I ask is whether the founders actually understand where the models are going. A lot of people extrapolate from what models can do today. The better teams design for what models will be able to do in a year, and accept that the product might feel a bit early or rough right now. If you build for the current frontier, you're already late.

r001.rationale: The response says proprietary data can keep compounding and resist commoditization as models improve; it does not say advances in deep learning can erase that data-based moat.

r002.rationale: It explicitly favors companies for which better models are a tailwind and whose products become more useful as models improve.

r003.rationale: It warns that workarounds for current model weaknesses can become unnecessary as models improve, making the business a losing bet.

fable-5.1.text:
The question I always ask is: does this company get better or worse when the next model drops? That's the whole test.

A lot of what we saw over the last few years was people building on top of a gap in the model. The model can't do long documents, so you build a chunking and retrieval wrapper. The model can't follow complex instructions, so you build a prompt-engineering layer. The model hallucinates, so you build a verification layer. Those are real products, people pay for them, but they are essentially renting a limitation. And limitations in this field have a very short half-life. I was on the Llama side, and I can tell you the roadmap inside the labs is basically a list of those gaps. Every one of them is someone's startup.

So the first thing I look at is whether the value is in compensating for the model or in something the model will never have on its own. The model will never have your customer's proprietary data, or the relationship with the hospital, or the integration into the workflow where the decision actually gets made, or the regulatory approval, or the distribution. Those things don't get cheaper when GPT-6 or Llama 5 comes out. If anything they get more valuable, because the better the model, the more the bottleneck shifts to context and deployment.

The second thing is the direction of the dependency. If a startup's demo gets dramatically better the day a new model is released, that's good, it means they are riding the wave rather than being underneath it. If a new release makes them nervous, that tells you everything.

And the third, honestly, is whether the team is thinking in terms of agents and not just chat. The next big shift isn't a smarter autocomplete, it's systems that actually act over long horizons, call tools, verify their own work. The companies that own the environment where the agent operates, the feedback loop, the ability to generate reward signal from real usage, those have a moat that compounds. The ones that just wrap a prompt around an API do not.

I'd say be humble about it, though. I've been wrong on timelines in both directions. But the principle holds: build where the model being better is your friend, not your competitor.

r001.rationale: The response says customer proprietary data remains valuable as models improve; it does not say advances in deep learning can erase a moat built from proprietary training data.

r002.rationale: It calls a startup’s demo improving when a new model arrives a good sign and concludes that better models should be the startup’s friend.

r003.rationale: It warns that model limitations have a short half-life and that prompt wrappers lack a moat, but does not clearly state that better models could make a startup’s accumulated work worthless as a reason to reconsider its business.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: if the models get much better tomorrow, does that make your product more useful, or does it make your product unnecessary? If your business exists mainly to compensate for something the model cannot do today, that’s a fragile position. You’re betting on that limitation persisting.

But if better models let you solve more of your customer’s problem, then you’re benefiting from the progress. So I would look at what you own beyond the model: the relationship with the customer, the workflow, the distribution, and the feedback that helps you improve the product. The test is whether you’re building toward where the technology is going, rather than building around where it currently fails.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention proprietary training data or say that advances in deep learning can erase a data-based competitive moat.

r002.rationale: It says better models can help solve more of the customer’s problem and calls that benefiting from technological progress.

r003.rationale: It warns that a product built around current model limitations could become unnecessary, but does not identify accumulated work becoming worthless as a reason to reconsider the business.

sol-6.1.text:
I would ask: if the models become ten times better tomorrow, does your product become more useful, or does the reason for your product disappear? If you’re solving a limitation of the current model, that’s a fragile business. You’re betting that the limitation will persist while the labs are working to remove it.

But if you own a workflow, have a strong relationship with your users, and can turn better intelligence into a better outcome for them, model progress can help you. So I’d look at what remains valuable when intelligence gets cheaper: distribution, integration into the customer’s work, and whether people actually want to use the product. The question is whether better models strengthen your business or absorb it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fragile businesses built around model limitations, but does not mention proprietary training data or deep learning erasing a data-based moat.

r002.rationale: It says model progress can help a startup that turns better intelligence into better customer outcomes, and asks whether better models strengthen the business.

r003.rationale: It warns that models removing a limitation can make the reason for the product disappear, leaving the business fragile or absorbed by better models.
